also: how long until we get there?

terms.gloss: how many days’ journey is it?
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.3.191: videō quot diērum via sit
terms.comment: Latin measures a journey by the days (or hours) it takes, in the genitive.

terms.gloss: how many hours is the journey?
terms.comment: Cicero’s question with hours, for a short trip.

terms.gloss: how soon will we get there?
terms.comment: The child’s question on the way, on the pattern of Plautus’s quam mox nāvigō?.

phrases.latin: Quam mox perveniēmus? — Mox. Vidēsne jam urbem?
phrases.english: How long till we get there? — Not long. Can you see the town yet?

phrases.latin: quam mox nāvigō in Ephesum, ut aurum repetam ab Theotīmō domum?
phrases.english: how soon do I sail for Ephesus, to fetch the gold home from Theotimus?

phrases.latin: videō quid inter annōnam interesse soleat, videō quot diērum via sit
phrases.english: I see what the difference in the price of grain usually is, I see how many days’ journey it is

phrases.latin: Quam mox cocta erit placenta? — Intrā sēmihōram.
phrases.english: How long will the cake take? — Less than half an hour.

sources: Lewis & Short: quot · Lewis & Short: dies · Lewis & Short: mox
